claim: Mice are an instructive tool for the study of human metabolism as they can mirror human physiology in their responses to age-related and diet-induced obesity, and their physiological compensations to resist weight loss.
source: Mice are an instructive tool for the study of human metabolism as they can mirror human physiology in their responses to age-related and diet-induced obesity, and their physiological compensations to resist weight loss (Speakman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Speakman et al., 2007

claim: The study of genetic and environmental factors influencing energy balance using laboratory animals has been advanced by the introduction of indirect calorimetry systems.
source: The study of genetic and environmental factors influencing energy balance using laboratory animals has been advanced by the introduction of indirect calorimetry systems (Even and Nadkarni, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Even and Nadkarni, 2012

claim: Indirect calorimeters measure metabolic rates using gas sensors to capture rates of change in O2 consumption and CO2 production within an open flow system.
source: Indirect calorimeters measure metabolic rates using gas sensors to capture rates of change in O2 consumption and CO2 production within an open flow system.
evidence: Describes established methodology for indirect calorimetry

claim: Weight gain results when food intake outpaces metabolic rate.
source: Weight gain results when food intake outpaces metabolic rate.
evidence: Based on established principles of energy balance

claim: When food intake falls below metabolic rate, weight loss ensues.
source: Inversely, when food intake falls below metabolic rate, weight loss ensues.
evidence: Based on established principles of energy balance

claim: Comparing results from published indirect calorimetry studies has been hampered by inconsistent application of analytical techniques.
source: However, comparing results from published indirect calorimetry studies has been hampered by inconsistent application of analytical techniques.
evidence: Supported by subsequent citations to literature on this issue

claim: In studies of obesity, metabolic rates of mice with different body compositions are sometimes subjected to inappropriate normalization attempts.
source: In studies of obesity, metabolic rates of mice with different body compositions are sometimes subjected to inappropriate normalization attempts (Arch et al., 2006; Katch, 1972; Kleiber, 1932; Tanner, 1949).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Many groups have agreed that the optimal data treatment uses the ANCOVA, an ANOVA with body mass or body composition as a covariate.
source: Many groups have agreed that the optimal data treatment uses the ANCOVA, an ANOVA with body mass or body composition as a covariate (Arch et al., 2006; Kaiyala, 2020; Kaiyala, 2014; Kaiyala et al., 2010; Kaiyala and Schwartz, 2011; Speakman et al., 2013; Tschöp et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to methodological papers

claim: The implementation of ANCOVA recommendations has been uneven.
source: However, the implementation of these recommendations has been uneven (Fernández-Verdejo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernández-Verdejo et al., 2019

claim: CalR facilitates investigators uploading and analyzing their calorimetry data by automating many of the routine steps of data curation, pre-defining statistical significance cutoffs, and allowing users to automatically perform appropriate statistical tests for interaction effects.
source: To address this problem, we developed CalR, which facilitates investigators uploading and analyzing their calorimetry data by automating many of the routine steps of data curation, pre-defining statistical significance cutoffs, and allowing users to automatically perform appropriate statistical tests for interaction effects (Mina et al., 2018).
evidence: Describes the authors' own tool with citation

claim: CalR is the first step toward standardization of indirect calorimetry analysis across different equipment platforms.
source: CalR is the first step toward standardization of indirect calorimetry analysis across different equipment platforms.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their tool's role

claim: Weekly body masses were similar among institutions for mice on LFD but diverged significantly among mice on HFD.
source: Weekly body masses were similar among institutions for mice on LFD but diverged significantly among mice on HFD (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Regression plots of 24 hr average energy expenditure (EE) versus total body mass showed distinct site-specific metabolic rates which could be attributed to differences in body mass for mice on LFD or HFD.
source: Regression plots of 24 hr average energy expenditure (EE) versus total body mass showed distinct site-specific metabolic rates which could be attributed to differences in body mass for mice on LFD or HFD (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Mice at each site and overall had a positive association between mass and EE.
source: Mice at each site and overall had a positive association between mass and EE.
evidence: Derived from analysis of the MMPC data

claim: The mass effect reflects the biological consequence of Newton's 2nd law of motion, whereby movement of greater mass requires more energy, and by extension larger animals require more energy for both resting metabolism and to perform work under standard conditions.
source: This mass effect reflects the biological consequence of Newton's 2nd law of motion, whereby movement of greater mass requires more energy, and by extension larger animals require more energy for both resting metabolism and to perform work under standard conditions (Kleiber, 1932; White and Seymour, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational work on metabolic scaling

claim: For mice on LFD, animals at each institution formed distinct slopes and intercepts indicative of location-specific differences in housing temperature, experimental apparatus, microbiome, and other factors.
source: For mice on LFD, animals at each institution formed distinct slopes and intercepts indicative of location-specific differences in housing temperature, experimental apparatus, microbiome, and other factors.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in regression parameters across sites

claim: For animals on 4 or 11 weeks of HFD, we observed identical slopes with different intercepts.
source: For animals on 4 or 11 weeks of HFD, we observed identical slopes with different intercepts (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The relationship of EE to mass among genetically identical mice is similar despite absolute differences in EE at different locations.
source: This suggests that the relationship of EE to mass among genetically identical mice is similar despite absolute differences in EE at different locations.

claim: An unexpectedly large weight variation was observed by site among the 30 mice randomly assigned to HFD.

claim: Body masses and compositions diverged appreciably, both among institutions and within each site's colony.
source: Body masses and compositions diverged appreciably, both among institutions and within each site's colony.
evidence: Observed in the MMPC experiment data

claim: The mass variation was not observed for mice on LFD, suggesting strong effects driving obesity which are not encoded by genetic variation in C57BL/6 mice.

claim: Rodents engage in a behavioral response when challenged with a novel environment.

source: In this study, locomotor activity was not significantly impacted by lack of acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).

source: Overall, lack of acclimation adds a small but unpredictable level of noise and variation to the measurements tested.

claim: Both male and female C57BL/6 mice typically gain weight on a diet high in fat.
